name: Neem (Azadirachta indica)
short: Neem seed oil poisoning, mostly in infants and young children (swallowed in one series): toxic encephalopathy, seizures, deaths reported (case reports). On the skin: contact dermatitis (case reports).
text: The serious harms come from case reports of poisoning with neem seed oil (margosa oil); the 1981 infant series describes it being swallowed, the 1990 report says it is often given by mouth to infants but does not say how its two infants were exposed, and two later case reports of neem oil poisoning do not state the route. A 1990 report of two infants states that margosa oil, a traditional medicine used in South and Southeast Asia that is often given by mouth to newborns and infants in small amounts, causes toxic encephalopathy (brain poisoning) particularly in infants and young children, with vomiting, drowsiness, fast breathing and repeated seizures; prognosis is usually good, but deaths and neurological deficits have been reported. In a 1981 series, thirteen infants developed vomiting, drowsiness, metabolic acidosis and encephalopathy within hours of swallowing margosa oil; a liver biopsy in one infant and post-mortem examination of mice given the oil experimentally showed pronounced fatty infiltration of the liver and kidney tubules and brain swelling (cerebral oedema), with mitochondrial damage on electron microscopy (the abstract does not separate the infant's findings from the mice's); the authors suggested the oil may be involved in Reye's syndrome. A 5-year-old child had seizures that did not respond to treatment, with later hearing, vision and balance problems, and an elderly man had vomiting, seizures and toxic encephalopathy before recovering fully (case reports). Applied to the skin, neem oil has caused contact dermatitis (allergic in one report; in another, an acute contact dermatitis of the scalp and face after use for hair loss, which the abstract does not call allergic), and a man developed a hypopigmented (pale) rash after 6 months of repeated application (case reports). A review of human and animal data on neem preparations taken by mouth, written about neem-based pesticides, found that reversible effects on reproduction in both male and female mammals were the most important toxic effects of longer exposure. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
